learn.hook: Your class has 40 marks scribbled on a page. In two minutes, can you say how many scored above 30? Organise the data and you can!
points: Data are facts or numbers collected for a purpose. Data you collect yourself are primary data; data taken from records or other sources are secondary data.
Raw data are data not yet arranged. Range = highest value − lowest value.
A frequency table shows how often each value (or group of values) occurs. Tally marks help you count.
For large data, use classes like 10–20, 20–30. Class width = upper limit − lower limit; class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.
In classes such as 10–20 and 20–30, a value of exactly 20 is counted in 20–30 (the lower limit is included).

example.q: Marks of 12 students (out of 20): 12, 15, 8, 18, 15, 11, 9, 15, 17, 12, 6, 14. Make a frequency table with classes 5–10, 10–15, 15–20.

learn.reallife: The Census of India collects data from crores of households and organises it into tables so the government can plan schools, roads and hospitals.

games.title: Data words
pairs: How many times a value occurs

games.title: Primary or secondary data?
items: Heights you measure of your classmates
A survey you run on favourite snacks
Temperatures you record each morning
Your own count of cars passing the school gate
Population figures from the Census website
Rainfall data from a newspaper
Cricket scores from a sports magazine
Exam results published by the school

quiz.q: What is the range of the data 12, 7, 19, 3, 15?
quiz.explain: Range = highest − lowest = 19 − 3 = 16.
quiz.mistake: Gives the highest value instead of the difference

quiz.q: What is the class mark of the class 20–30?
quiz.explain: Class mark = (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25, the middle of the class.
quiz.mistake: Gives the class width (10) or the sum of the limits (50)

quiz.q: What is the width of the class 45–60?
quiz.explain: Class width = upper limit − lower limit = 60 − 45 = 15.
quiz.mistake: Gives the class mark (52.5) instead of the width

quiz.q: Test scores of 10 students: 6, 8, 9, 5, 8, 10, 7, 8, 9, 4. How many students scored 8 or more?
quiz.explain: The scores 8 or more are 8, 9, 8, 10, 8 and 9: six students.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the scores above 8, leaving out the 8s

quiz.q: Classes are 0–10, 10–20, 20–30. In which class is a value of exactly 10 counted?
quiz.explain: In these classes the lower limit is included and the upper limit is not, so 10 goes into 10–20.
quiz.mistake: Counts a boundary value twice or in the lower class

quiz.q: Harpreet asks her classmates about their favourite festival and records the answers. What kind of data is this?
quiz.explain: She collected the data herself, first-hand, so it is primary data.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary data must come from an official source

quiz.q: A frequency table for the number of siblings shows frequencies 5, 8, 12, 7 and 3. How many students were surveyed?
quiz.explain: The total number of students is the sum of the frequencies: 5 + 8 + 12 + 7 + 3 = 35.
quiz.mistake: Gives the largest frequency or the number of rows in the table

quiz.q: Kabir groups heights from 140 cm to 170 cm into classes of width 5 cm (140–145, 145–150, ...). How many classes does he need?
quiz.explain: The data cover 170 − 140 = 30 cm, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6 classes.
quiz.mistake: Counts the boundary points (7) instead of the gaps between them

teach.ask: Gappu has 50 numbers written in a messy list: "How can I make sense of all of them?"
teach.praise: Group the values into classes and count how many fall in each, using tally marks. A neat frequency table at last!
teach.nudge: What could you count to make the list easier to read? Could you put the values into groups?

learn.hook: Your cricket team's scores were 12, 15, 9 and 120. Was the team's 'typical' score really 39? Different averages tell different stories!
points: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
For a frequency table: mean = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf, where x is each value and f its frequency.
Median: arrange the data in order. For an odd count it is the middle value; for an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
Mode is the value that occurs most often.
One very large or very small value (an outlier) pulls the mean a lot but hardly changes the median.

example.q: Find the mean and median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 3, 11.

learn.reallife: News reports often give the median house price or median salary, because a few very rich people would push the mean up a lot.

items.text: To find the median, first arrange the data in ___
The value that occurs most often is the ___
Sum of values ÷ number of values gives the ___
One very large value changes the ___ much more than the median

quiz.q: Find the mean of 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7.
quiz.explain: Sum = 35 and there are 5 values, so the mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives the sum without dividing, or picks the middle value of the unsorted list

quiz.q: Find the median of 3, 9, 1, 7, 6.
quiz.explain: In order: 1, 3, 6, 7, 9. The middle (3rd) value is 6.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle of the unsorted list (1) without arranging the data first

quiz.q: Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
quiz.explain: There are 6 values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the two middle values instead of their mean

quiz.q: Riya scored 72, 85, 90 and 78 in four tests. What must she score in the fifth test to make her mean exactly 80?
quiz.explain: For a mean of 80 over 5 tests she needs a total of 400. So far she has 325, so she needs 75.
quiz.mistake: Assumes she needs the target mean itself (80) in the last test

quiz.q: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 5?
quiz.explain: 3 occurs three times, more than any other value.
quiz.mistake: Finds the mean (4) instead of the most frequent value

quiz.q: In a class survey, 4 students have 1 pet, 3 have 2 pets and 3 have 3 pets. What is the mean number of pets?
quiz.mistake: Just averages the values 1, 2, 3 and ignores the frequencies, getting 2

quiz.q: Monthly pocket money of five friends: ₹200, ₹220, ₹250, ₹230 and ₹2000. Which average best shows what is typical?
options: The mean, because it uses every value
The median, because the mean is pulled up by one very large value
quiz.explain: The mean is ₹580, which is more than four of the five friends get. The median ₹230 is much more typical.
quiz.mistake: Always trusts the mean, even when there is an outlier

quiz.q: The mean of 10 numbers is 15. Later it is found that 24 was wrongly copied as 42. What is the correct mean?
quiz.explain: The wrong total is 150. The correct total is 150 − 42 + 24 = 132, so the correct mean is 13.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the difference of 18 instead of subtracting it, getting 16.8

teach.ask: Gappu has the numbers 5, 1, 9, 3, 7: "How do I find the mean and the median? Aren't they the same thing?"
teach.praise: Mean: add them up and divide by how many (25 ÷ 5 = 5). Median: arrange in order and take the middle one (also 5 here, but not always the same!).
teach.nudge: For the median, what do you do with the numbers before picking the middle one?

learn.hook: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! But a sneaky graph can also trick your eyes. Let's learn to read graphs like a detective.
points: Bar graphs show separate categories with bars of equal width and equal gaps between them.
A histogram shows grouped (continuous) data. The bars touch each other because the classes have no gaps.
If the classes in a histogram have unequal widths, adjust the heights so that the area of each bar is proportional to its frequency.
A frequency polygon is made by joining the mid-points (class marks) of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.
Line graphs show change over time. Always check the scale: an axis that does not start at 0 can make small differences look huge.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–40 have frequencies 6, 9 and 12. What heights should the histogram bars have if a width of 10 is the standard?
steps: 0–10 and 10–20 have width 10, so heights stay 6 and 9
20–40 has width 20, twice the standard width

learn.reallife: Weather reports use line graphs for temperature, election coverage uses bar graphs, and doctors use histograms of patients' ages.

games.title: Pick the right graph
pairs: Temperature every hour of a day
Joining class marks of a histogram

games.title: Graph detective
items: In a histogram, there are no gaps between the bars
The classes are continuous, so each bar starts where the previous one ends.
In a bar graph the bars may have different widths
Bar graphs use equal widths so only the heights matter.
A frequency polygon joins the class marks of the bar tops
Each point is plotted at the middle of its class.
A graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 can make a small difference look big
Cutting off the bottom of the bars exaggerates the difference between them.
A line graph is the best way to show the favourite colours of a class
Favourite colours are separate categories, so a bar graph suits them better.

quiz.q: Why do the bars of a histogram touch each other?
options: To save space on the page
Because the classes are continuous with no gaps between them
Because it is a line graph
quiz.explain: In a histogram each class ends exactly where the next one begins, so the bars sit side by side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a histogram is just a bar graph drawn closer together

quiz.q: In a frequency polygon, each frequency is plotted against which value of its class?
quiz.explain: The points of a frequency polygon are at the class marks, the middle of each class.
quiz.mistake: Plots each point at the start of the class

quiz.q: Tickets sold at a school fair: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40, Fri 30. What is the difference between the highest and lowest day's sales?
quiz.explain: Highest is Thursday (40) and lowest is Wednesday (15): 40 − 15 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Uses Monday as the lowest because it comes first

items: Mon
Tue
Wed
Thu
Fri

quiz.q: Monthly rainfall in a town: June 120 mm, July 300 mm, August 240 mm, September 150 mm. In which month was the rainfall exactly twice that of June?
quiz.explain: Twice June's rainfall is 2 × 120 = 240 mm, which is August.
quiz.mistake: Picks the tallest bar (July) without checking the numbers

items: Jun
Jul
Aug
Sep

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing how the temperature changed hour by hour on a day?
options: A bar graph of favourite colours
quiz.explain: A line graph joins readings taken over time, making rises and falls easy to see.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a histogram, which is for grouped data, not changes over time

quiz.q: A bar graph compares two shops' sales of 92 and 96 sweets, but its vertical axis starts at 90. Why does it look misleading?
options: The bars are the wrong colour
The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks very large
quiz.explain: Starting at 90, the bars look like 2 and 6 units tall, so one seems three times the other, though 96 is barely more than 92.
quiz.mistake: Reads only the heights of the bars without checking the scale

quiz.q: In a histogram, class 0–10 has frequency 5 and class 10–30 has frequency 20. Taking width 10 as standard, what should the adjusted height of the 10–30 bar be?
quiz.explain: The class 10–30 is twice the standard width, so its height is halved: 20 × 10 ÷ 20 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Uses the frequency as the height even though the class is wider

quiz.q: A bar graph shows Riya sold 45 laddoos and Meena sold 62 laddoos at the Diwali stall. How many more did Meena sell?
quiz.explain: Difference = 62 − 45 = 17 laddoos.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two bars instead of finding the difference

teach.ask: Gappu looks at two graphs: "Why are the bars in a histogram stuck together, but not in a bar graph?"
teach.praise: A histogram shows continuous classes, so its bars touch. A bar graph shows separate categories, so it has gaps. Got it!
teach.nudge: Is there any gap between the classes 10–20 and 20–30? What about between 'cricket' and 'football'?
